meta.note: All descriptions are drawn directly from Tanit XR archive pages. Positions and placements belong to this experience, not the original site.

artifacts.title: Corinthian Capital
artifacts.what: An ornately carved stone column capital featuring the distinctive acanthus leaf motif of classical Corinthian architecture. Once crowned tall columns in temples, porticoes, and public buildings on Byrsa Hill.
artifacts.description: An ornately carved capital featuring the distinctive acanthus leaf motif characteristic of classical Corinthian architecture. The piece once crowned tall columns in temples, porticoes, and public buildings. Despite weathering, it retains its decorative richness. Scholarly analysis notes the Carthaginian geometric restraint in the acanthus carving as evidence of cultural hybridity — Roman form adapted through a local hand.
artifacts.significance: Illustrates Roman architectural sophistication and Mediterranean cultural influence. Provides insight into the monumental scale of Carthage's Roman forum. Evidence of cultural blending between North African and Roman artistic traditions.

artifacts.title: Roman Column
artifacts.what: A freestanding stone column that once formed part of the monumental Roman architecture dominating Byrsa Hill. Shows signs of erosion and chipping but its form remains largely intact.
artifacts.description: A freestanding column that once formed part of the monumental Roman architecture dominating Byrsa Hill. Shows signs of erosion and chipping, but its form remains intact. Supported temples, porticoes, and public buildings — the civic infrastructure of a city rebuilt in Rome's image after the Punic Wars.
artifacts.significance: Demonstrates the scale of Roman architectural achievement in ancient Carthage. Represents the cultural layering of Punic and Roman civilizations at the city's historic citadel.

artifacts.title: Roman Column Base
artifacts.what: A carved stone base that once supported a column in Roman Carthage. Features a circular top with layered moldings characteristic of Roman forums and temples. Shows weathering and cracks from long exposure.
artifacts.description: A carved stone column base from Byrsa Hill, Carthage, with a circular upper surface and layered mouldings.
artifacts.significance: Evidence of monumental Roman structures at Byrsa Hill. Reveals the scale and grandeur of the city's reconstruction after the Punic Wars.

artifacts.title: Fluted Column Fragment
artifacts.what: A fragment of a fluted stone column from Byrsa Hill, the ancient citadel of Carthage. The hill once served as the city's political and religious center before hosting Roman monumental architecture.
artifacts.description: A fragment of a fluted stone column from Byrsa Hill, the ancient citadel of Carthage. The hill once served as the city's political and religious center before hosting Roman monumental architecture. The fluting — vertical grooves running the length of the shaft — is a hallmark of classical column design carried west across the Mediterranean.
artifacts.significance: Represents the layered history of Carthage, exemplifying the transition from Punic to Roman occupation. Evidence of cultural blending and architectural continuity across civilizations.

artifacts.title: Roman Togatus Statue
artifacts.what: A headless marble sculpture depicting a Roman figure in formal toga dress. The detailed folds of the garment symbolize civic duty and elite status in Roman society.
artifacts.description: A headless marble sculpture depicting a Roman figure in formal toga dress (togatus). The detailed folds of the garment symbolize civic duty and elite status in Roman society. The head and some arm portions are missing — losses accumulated over centuries of exposure and repurposing. The toga itself was a marker of citizenship and belonging to the Roman world.
artifacts.significance: Represents cultural blending following the Punic Wars. Exemplifies how Roman colonization incorporated new artistic standards into conquered territory, transforming Carthage's civic identity.

artifacts.title: Roman Draped Statue
artifacts.what: A fragmentary marble sculpture depicting a Roman figure in heavy drapery. The head and arms are missing, but the garment's folds retain remarkable detail, reflecting the craftsmanship of Roman sculptors.
artifacts.description: A fragmentary marble sculpture depicting a Roman figure in heavy drapery. The head and arms are missing, but the garment's folds retain remarkable detail, reflecting the craftsmanship of Roman sculptors. The stance conveys dignity and public importance — qualities Roman portrait sculpture was designed to communicate to passersby.
artifacts.significance: Exemplifies Roman colonization of Carthage. Represents citizens or officials, symbolizing the city's transformation from Punic stronghold to Roman metropolis.

artifacts.title: Draped Statue
artifacts.what: A marble statue representing a youthful figure in a long draped garment, typical of Roman portrait sculpture. Reflects the Roman influence on art and public space after the city's reconstruction. The exact identity of the depicted figure is unknown.
artifacts.description: A marble statue representing a youthful figure in a long draped garment, typical of Roman portrait sculpture. Reflects the Roman influence on the city's art and public space after its reconstruction. The exact identity of the depicted figure is unknown — it may represent a civic official, a deity, or a wealthy patron.
artifacts.significance: Reflects Roman influence on art and public space in reconstructed Carthage. The unknown identity adds archaeological interest — one of many figures whose stories the centuries have erased.

artifacts.title: Headless Draped Statue
artifacts.what: A Roman statue featuring draped clothing in the Togatus style, though its specific identity remains undetermined. The head is missing.
artifacts.description: A Roman statue featuring draped clothing in the Togatus style, though its specific identity remains undetermined. The head is missing, lost to time or deliberate removal — a recurring fate for portrait statues whose subjects fell from favor or were stripped for raw material.
artifacts.significance: Represents an important cultural artifact from ancient Carthage. The absence of the head, so common among surviving Roman sculpture, speaks to the fragility of individual identity across millennia.

artifacts.title: Reclining Figure
artifacts.what: A funerary sculpture depicting the deceased in a peaceful reclining pose, a form common in both Roman and Punic funerary art. Likely a sarcophagus lid decoration.
artifacts.description: A funerary sculpture depicting the deceased in a peaceful reclining pose, a form commonly seen in Roman and Punic funerary art. The artifact reflects cultural blending between Carthaginian and Roman traditions — both civilizations used reclining figures to honor their dead, each inflecting the form with their own symbolic vocabulary.
artifacts.significance: Provides insight into funerary practices and the cultural blending that occurred in Carthage. The shared iconographic form across Punic and Roman traditions reveals the depth of Mediterranean cultural exchange.

artifacts.title: Inscribed Architectural Fragment
artifacts.what: A broken stone block preserving part of a Latin inscription alongside decorative moldings featuring floral and bead patterns. Once part of a significant Roman structure or commemorative monument.
artifacts.description: A broken stone block preserving part of a Latin inscription alongside decorative moldings. Features surviving floral and bead pattern designs, suggesting it was once part of a significant Roman structure or commemorative monument. The inscription fragment hints at an official dedication — to an emperor, a deity, or a patron whose name the break has swallowed.
artifacts.significance: Contributes to understanding of Roman Carthage's architectural landscape and public spaces. Demonstrates how Romans integrated decorative and textual elements in monumental architecture, potentially honoring emperors, officials, or deities.

artifacts.title: Roman Mosaic with Bird and Vine Motifs
artifacts.what: A floor mosaic panel composed of tesserae depicting a bird perched among vines, grapes, and leaves. Exemplifies Roman domestic decoration themes of abundance and fertility.
artifacts.description: A mosaic panel featuring a bird perched among vines, grapes, and leaves. Exemplifies Roman domestic decoration themes of abundance and fertility. Demonstrates the expertise of Roman craftsmen who synthesized local materials with Mediterranean artistic traditions — tiny tiles assembled into an image of natural plenty for a household floor.
artifacts.significance: Adorned wealthy household floors, transforming domestic spaces into artistic displays. Reflects Roman artistic values and cultural sophistication in North Africa.

artifacts.title: Standing Draped Statue
artifacts.what: A headless and armless marble statue depicting a standing figure wrapped in flowing drapery. The carefully carved folds demonstrate movement and elegance, hallmarks of Roman sculptural style.
artifacts.description: A headless and armless marble statue depicting a standing figure wrapped in flowing drapery. The carefully carved folds demonstrate movement and elegance, hallmarks of Roman sculptural style. Such statues often stood in courtyards or garden niches, bringing life and presence into domestic spaces — silent guests in the homes of Carthage's Roman elite.
artifacts.significance: Reflects the artistic taste and cultural values of Carthage's Roman elite. Demonstrates how Roman domestic spaces blurred the boundary between home and public monument.

artifacts.title: Male Torso Statue
artifacts.what: A marble sculpture depicting a male figure in classical style, fragmentary — lacking the head, arms, and lower legs. The preserved torso displays the muscular form and proportions of Roman-Hellenistic idealized sculpture.
artifacts.findSite: Roman Villas of Carthage, Tunis, Tunisia
artifacts.description: A marble sculpture depicting a male figure in classical style. The piece is fragmentary, lacking the head, arms, and lower legs. The preserved torso displays the muscular form and proportions admired in Roman art, echoing Greek ideals of beauty and strength that traveled west through centuries of cultural exchange.
artifacts.significance: Likely decorated domestic spaces, courtyards, and gardens within elite Roman households. Exemplifies Roman sculptural traditions influenced by Hellenistic aesthetics and represents the domestic decoration practices of ancient Carthage's prosperity.

artifacts.title: Bust Fragment
artifacts.what: A marble fragment preserving the back of the head and shoulders of a figure with visible drapery around the neck. The face and front section are missing.
artifacts.description: A fragment preserving the back of the head and shoulders of a figure with visible drapery around the neck. The face and front section are missing due to deterioration or historical loss. We see only what the earth chose to preserve: the curve of the neck, the fall of cloth, the anonymous back of someone's memorial.
artifacts.significance: Sculptures of this type were common in Roman domestic spaces, often used to commemorate ancestors, honor public figures, or serve as decorative art in private villas. Demonstrates Roman attention to portraiture and individual representation.

artifacts.title: Decorated Bust Fragment
artifacts.what: A sculpted bust fragment preserving the upper torso richly decorated with relief figures and carved patterns on the chest and shoulders. Head and arms are missing. The elaborate ornamentation suggests a cult object or high-status display piece.
artifacts.description: A sculpted bust fragment preserving the upper torso richly decorated with relief figures and patterns. Features carved scenes on the chest and shoulders, potentially depicting mythological figures or symbolic elements. The head and arms are missing. Unlike a simple portrait bust, the elaborate relief work suggests this piece belonged to a specific display context — perhaps linked to a cult, a deity, or a formal commemoration.
artifacts.significance: The decorated nature distinguishes this from typical villa statuary. The carved scenes indicate higher-status usage within private villa settings, possibly connected to religious practice or elite identity display.

artifacts.title: Statue Fragment
artifacts.what: A marble torso representing the remains of a draped statue with visible garment folds. Missing its head and lower body. Likely adorned elite residences or gardens in ancient Carthage.
artifacts.description: A marble torso representing the remains of a draped statue with visible garment folds. Missing its head and lower body. Likely adorned elite residences or gardens in ancient Carthage — one of many fragments that once formed a complete human presence, now surviving only as evidence of what was.
artifacts.significance: Demonstrates the domestic luxury and artistic culture of Carthage as a prosperous Roman colony. Served both decorative and symbolic functions within wealthy households.

artifacts.title: Bird of Prey Statue
artifacts.what: A weathered stone sculpture depicting a bird of prey with folded wings and a curved beak, likely an eagle. The eagle embodied strength, divinity, and imperial authority in Roman symbolic iconography.
artifacts.findSite: Roman Villas of Carthage, Tunis, Tunisia
artifacts.description: A weathered stone sculpture depicting a bird of prey with folded wings and a curved beak, likely an eagle. The eagle embodied strength, divinity, and the authority of the empire in Roman symbolic iconography. Here in a private villa garden, it watched over the household — guardian, symbol, and status display in one carved form.
artifacts.significance: Statues like this adorned the luxurious domestic spaces of Carthage, reflecting both artistic refinement and symbolic meaning. Demonstrates the decorative and ideological priorities of Roman elite households.

artifacts.title: Tanit Stela
artifacts.what: A narrow stone stela from the Tophet of Salammbô. Tanit XR identifies its carved geometric sign as the symbol of Tanit.
artifacts.description: A narrow stone stela from the Tophet of Salammbô. Tanit XR identifies its carved geometric sign as the symbol of Tanit.
artifacts.significance: Displayed alongside another Tophet stela in the existing garden collection.

artifacts.title: Punic Stela
artifacts.what: A limestone stela from the Tophet of Salammbô, originally displaying religious symbols — the sign of Tanit, crescent moons, or inscriptions — dedicated to the deities Tanit and Baal Hammon.
artifacts.description: A scanned limestone Punic stela from the Tophet of Salammbo in Carthage, identified by Tanit XR.
artifacts.significance: Serves as a powerful witness of Carthage's religious and cultural life. Demonstrates Carthaginian ritual practices and religious devotion. The Tophet remains one of the most debated archaeological sites in the ancient world.

artifacts.title: Punic Stelae Row
artifacts.what: A photogrammetry scan depicting a row of Punic limestone stelae from the Tophet of Salammbô. The stelae feature temple-like façades, religious symbols, and inscriptions dedicated to Tanit and Baal Hammon.
artifacts.description: A scan depicting a row of Punic stelae from the Tophet of Salammbo, a sacred sanctuary in ancient Carthage. The stelae are limestone carvings featuring temple-like façades, religious symbols, and inscriptions. Dedicated to the deities Tanit and Baal Hammon, they functioned both as offerings and as markers above urns containing cremated remains.
artifacts.significance: Provides insight into Carthaginian religious practices and the importance of Tanit as the city's protective goddess. The rows of stelae represent centuries of accumulated devotion — a landscape of grief and faith carved in stone.
artifacts.scanMethod: Photogrammetry using Scaniverse and Gaussian splats

artifacts.title: Carved Architectural Block with Laurel Motifs
artifacts.what: A decorated stone block with carved laurel patterns, once part of the ornamental architecture of the Water Temple at Zaghouan — the sacred source point of a Roman aqueduct that ran over 90 km north to supply ancient Carthage.
artifacts.description: A decorated stone block featuring carved laurel patterns, once part of the Water Temple's structural or ornamental elements. The laurel motifs symbolised triumph, eternity, and divine favour in Roman tradition. Now displaced from its original position, the block is a fragment of a temple that combined hydraulic engineering with sacred ritual — offerings and ceremonies took place here before water began its journey north to Carthage.
artifacts.significance: Originally part of the Water Temple that marked the starting point of the Zaghouan aqueduct, which transported water over 90 kilometres to Carthage. Demonstrates refined Roman stonecutting craftsmanship and the temple's dual purpose as hydraulic infrastructure and sacred site.

artifacts.title: Wooden Door with Tilework
artifacts.what: A preserved doorway featuring a heavy wooden door framed by intricate glazed ceramic tilework, from the Mausoleum of Sidi Sahbi in Kairouan. The carved wood and surrounding tiles blend Ottoman, Andalusian, and Tunisian decorative traditions.
artifacts.material: Wood (engraved with geometric and floral motifs); glazed ceramic tilework
artifacts.findSite: Mausoleum of Sidi Sahbi (Barber's Mosque), Kairouan, Tunisia
artifacts.description: A preserved doorway featuring a heavy wooden door framed by intricate glazed tilework, characteristic of Tunisian Islamic architectural decoration. The wooden panels show age-darkening and carved embellishments, while surrounding tiles display decorative star and floral patterning. The mausoleum honors a companion of the Prophet Muhammad and represents one of Kairouan's most venerated religious monuments. The door marked the threshold between the outer world and sacred space.
artifacts.significance: The craftsmanship demonstrates the blend of artistic traditions that flourished in Kairouan, one of Islam's earliest and most influential cities in North Africa. Reflects centuries of devotion concentrated into ornament.

artifacts.title: Marble Calligraphic Panel
artifacts.what: An ornamental marble panel intricately carved and inlaid with Qur'anic inscriptions in black script, framed by geometric motifs. Located outside the Zitouna Mosque in the Medina of Tunis.
artifacts.findSite: Outside Zitouna Mosque, Medina of Tunis, Tunisia
artifacts.description: An ornamental decorative panel intricately carved and inlaid with Qur'anic inscriptions in black script, framed by geometric motifs. Despite its fountain-like appearance, the panel serves purely decorative purposes. Represents the integration of sacred text into Tunisian Islamic architecture — the Word made permanent in stone.
artifacts.significance: Demonstrates the role of calligraphy as both a devotional act and an architectural feature, transforming sacred words into enduring stonework. A practice that treated writing itself as a form of worship.

artifacts.title: Bir (Traditional Well)
artifacts.what: A traditional Tunisian well featuring an ornate marble arch with alternating black-and-white voussoirs and vibrant geometric tilework in yellow, green, and blue. Used for water collection and storage in households, religious schools, and community spaces.
artifacts.description: A traditional Tunisian well featuring an ornate marble arch with alternating black-and-white voussoirs and intricate tilework in vibrant yellow, green, and blue geometric patterns. A deep circular stone basin serves water collection and storage for households, religious schools, and community spaces. Beyond practical function, the well carried symbolic meaning — representing purity, sustenance, and the communal sharing of resources.
artifacts.significance: Reflects Tunisian and Andalusian architectural influences layered over centuries of use. The Medina's wells were the social infrastructure of daily life, and their decoration signals the value the community placed on that shared resource.

artifacts.title: Ornamental Mihrab
artifacts.what: An ornamental niche drawing inspiration from mihrab design, featuring alternating black-and-white marble voussoirs, a carved plaster scallop shell, and richly patterned qallaline tiles. From Medersa Slimanya in the Medina of Tunis.
artifacts.material: Marble; carved plaster; qallaline ceramic tiles
artifacts.findSite: Medersa Slimanya, Medina of Tunis, Tunisia
artifacts.description: An ornamental niche drawing inspiration from mihrab design, featuring alternating black-and-white marble voussoirs, a carved plaster scallop shell, and richly patterned qallaline tiles with geometric and floral motifs. While visually echoing the spiritual significance of prayer niches, this element functions primarily as decoration within an educational building — the sacred aesthetic applied to a secular setting.
artifacts.significance: Reflects the Ottoman-Tunisian synthesis of architecture during the 18th century. Represents the decorative rather than devotional application of traditional Islamic architectural forms.

artifacts.title: Stone Basin
artifacts.what: A carved stone basin that functioned as part of the Roman hydraulic system at the Water Temple of Zaghouan, likely serving as a settling or distribution basin to collect and regulate spring water before it traveled along the aqueduct to Carthage.
artifacts.description: A carved stone basin that functioned as part of the Roman hydraulic system, likely serving as a settling or distribution basin to collect and regulate spring water before it traveled along the aqueduct to Carthage. A central perforated column may have controlled water flow and pressure. The aqueduct that began here ran over 90 kilometers north to supply the ancient city.
artifacts.significance: Exemplifies Roman hydraulic engineering innovation. Demonstrates how sacred worship spaces were integrated with functional infrastructure that supported entire cities. Reveals sophisticated understanding of water management and pressure control systems.

artifacts.title: Traditional Door
artifacts.what: A traditional Tunisian door showcasing intricate nail-studded motifs creating geometric and symbolic patterns. Heavy wood reinforced with metal studs and symmetrical iron knockers. Reflects layered Arab, Ottoman, and Andalusian craftsmanship.
artifacts.material: Heavy wood reinforced with metal studs; round iron knockers
artifacts.description: A traditional Tunisian door showcasing intricate nail-studded motifs creating geometric and symbolic patterns that reflect centuries-old artisanal techniques. The darker tone conveys strength through austere elegance. Symmetrically placed iron knockers demonstrate the balance between functionality and decorative artistry. The Medina's doors are among its most celebrated features — each one a household's public face.
artifacts.significance: Reflects layered influences of Arab, Ottoman, and Andalusian craftsmanship while adhering to local architectural traditions. In the Medina, a door announces a household's identity, pride, and place in the community.

artifacts.title: Traditional Loom with Woven Carpet
artifacts.what: A traditional loom carrying a partially woven textile.
artifacts.description: Tanit XR identifies this scan as a traditional loom with a partially woven carpet in the Medina of Tunis. The visible textile carries repeating green and beige diamond motifs.
artifacts.significance: Documents textile-making as part of Tunisia’s craft heritage.

artifacts.title: Tilework Wall Panel
artifacts.what: A scanned wall panel from Sidi Sahbi in Kairouan, combining a vase and plant motif in coloured ceramic tiles with a carved stucco surround.
artifacts.description: A scanned wall panel from Sidi Sahbi in Kairouan, combining a vase and plant motif in coloured ceramic tiles with a carved stucco surround.
artifacts.significance: Adds an original decorative surface to the existing study court.

artifacts.title: Architectural Relief Fragment
artifacts.what: A broken architectural block from the Water Temple at Zaghouan, preserving geometric relief and traces of plant ornament.
artifacts.description: A broken architectural block from the Water Temple at Zaghouan, preserving geometric relief and traces of plant ornament.
artifacts.period: Roman; Water Temple dated to the 2nd century CE
artifacts.significance: A comparative architectural exhibit inside the existing Roman precinct.
